connector: Harriet’s brothers turned back in the rain, so she decided to go alone. She left her quilt on the Quaker lady’s doorstep and sang goodbye as she walked past the cabins. Now she is heading north with the Quaker lady’s directions in her head and a note in her bag. Watch how she finds her way, by night and by day, and who helps her.

a.raw: the woods were darker than the open fields the road was more dangerous too
a.fixed: The woods were darker than the open fields. The road was more dangerous too.
a.why: Capital T to start; a period after fields ends the first thought, and capital T starts the second; the comparatives darker and more dangerous each compare two things.

b.raw: the open road was more dangerous than the woods harriet hid behind the bushes
b.fixed: The open road was more dangerous than the woods. Harriet hid behind the bushes.
b.why: Capital T to start; a period after woods ends the first thought; capital H on the name Harriet; the comparative more dangerous compares the road and the woods.

fill1.h1: You watch shows on it: pictures sent from somewhere else. Which part means far?
fill1.why: tele- means far: tele + vision = seeing from far away.

fill2.h1: Through this, the North Star would look much closer. Which part means far?
fill2.why: tele- means far: tele + scope = a tool for seeing far.

fill3.h1: A door that opens all by itself when you walk up. Which part means self?
fill3.why: auto- means self: auto + matic = works by itself.

fill4.h1: A life story written by the person who lived it. Which part means self?
fill4.why: auto- means self: auto + biography = a life story you write about yourself. Freedom Train is a biography, written by someone else.

g4w21cf1.h1: Two stretches of the night are being compared. Which ending is for comparing two?
g4w21cf1.why: colder: add -er to a short adjective when you compare two things.

g4w21cf2.h1: This night is compared to every other night of her life. Which ending is for the most of all?
g4w21cf2.why: longest: add -est when you compare one thing to all the others.

g4w21cf3.h1: Dangerous is a long word. Does it get an ending, or a helper word in front?
g4w21cf3.why: more dangerous: long adjectives use more instead of -er.

g4w21cf4.h1: Harriet is compared to every conductor in the group. Watch the e at the end of the base word.
g4w21cf4.why: bravest: brave already ends in e, so add only -st. The -est ending means the most of a whole group.

s4w21cf1.h1: Act already ends in t. Does anything need to change before the ending?
s4w21cf1.why: action: act + ion. Nothing changes; the -ion snaps right on.

s4w21cf2.h1: Think of the family divide and division. What happens to the d-e at the end?
s4w21cf2.why: decision: the -de becomes -s before -ion, just like divide and division.

s4w21cf3.h1: Think of the family admit and admission. What happens to the t?
s4w21cf3.why: permission: the t becomes ss before -ion, just like admit and admission.

s4w21cf4.h1: Discuss already ends in two s’s. Does anything need to change?
s4w21cf4.why: discussion: discuss + ion. The ss stays, and the -ion snaps on.

notes.wgrd: A true story moves through time. Look for time clues like the moon low in the sky, the midday sun, or midnight. Keep track of the miles too. When the routine breaks, a new step begins.
vocab: The order in which events happened, from first to last.
A personal account of what someone has seen or done.
The act of being set free.
notes.wordParts: tele- means “far” or “far away,” and auto- means “self”: telescope, television, automatic, autograph, autobiography.
notes.grammar: A comparative adjective compares two things: darker, more dangerous. Long words use more instead of -er. A good comparison also says how: the road was more dangerous because people could see her.
notes.spelling: Sometimes -ion just snaps on: act, action. Other times the end of the word changes first: decide, decision. Learn the word families, like divide and division. They help more than any rule.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. At the end of Chapter 6, Harriet left her quilt on the Quaker lady’s doorstep and walked away singing. Now she’s on her own. In Chapter 7, the North Star is her guide. But a star only shines at night. Today’s question: when daylight comes and the star is gone, how does Harriet still find her way north?
transcripts.guide2: Freedom Watch: the help of strangers. Harriet walks this whole chapter by herself, but she isn’t really alone. Some of her helpers aren’t even there. They gave her directions, or taught her something years ago. Others she meets for the very first time. In my research, I keep finding the same thing: almost every escape had helpers along the way. Count every one you find.
transcripts.read: Chapter 7 is one long journey, so keep a clock in your head. The moon, the sun, and the stars all tell you the time. I grew up near the Choptank, and it changes as you follow it upstream. Notice how it changes for Harriet, and why she walks in the water. Near the end, watch what she decides at a dark house.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: something far away, or your own self?

why.t: In Chapter 5, Harriet pieces together scraps of cloth into her own patchwork quilt, as warm and beautiful as her mother’s. Alone in the cabin, she pulls it around her shoulders and looks for the North Star through the cracks in the roof. In Chapter 6, she lays it on the Quaker lady’s doorstep: thank you, and farewell. tele- means far, and auto- means self. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. tele- = far, auto- = self.
